articles.title: Meta is opening pop-up shops to show off its smart glasses with a display
articles.summary: Meta is launching Meta Lab pop-up shops in Las Vegas, Los Angeles, and New York, where you’ll be able to try the Meta Ray-Ban Display smart glasses.
articles.body: Meta is just about to launch its impressive smart glasses with a display, and to give more people a chance to try them out and see its other smart glasses and VR hardware, the company is going to open new shops starting in October. New Meta Lab pop-up shops will be located in Las Vegas and New York, and and its Los Angeles Meta Lab location, which opened as a pop-up last year, will return as Meta’s flagship store. Meta’s Bay Area shop in Burlingame, California, remains open, too. Here’s when you’ll be able to visit each of the new stores, according to Meta: * The Las Vegas shop at the Wynn Las Vegas will open on October 16th * The Los Angeles shop on Melrose Avenue will open on October 24th, and it will be expanded to more than 20,000 square feet * The New York shop on Fifth Avenue is “currently scheduled” to open on November 13th And if you want to try out the Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses, you can book a demo on Meta’s website. For the Meta Labs stores, Meta will initially open up booking for demos at the Burlingame and Los Angeles locations. The website also has booking options for non-Meta Lab stores, but Meta says that appointments in “many major cities” are already booked through mid-October. The $799 Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses are set to launch on September 30th. Meta also recently released a second-generation version of the Ray-Ban Meta glasses and is scheduled to launch the $499 Oakley Meta Vanguard glasses on October 21st. Correction, September 24th: The Los Angeles store is being brought back as a permanent location, not a pop-up shop.

articles.title: Mint Mobile’s prepaid home internet plan is really cheap under very specific circumstances
articles.summary: Mint Mobile’s $30 a month prepaid 5G home internet is only $30 a month under very specific circumstances.
articles.body: Mint Mobile is trying something a bit less “mobile” with its new prepaid 5G home internet plan that goes for as little as $30 a month. To get that price, you will need to also have a Mint phone plan and pay for at least three months up front. But it’s still one of the cheapest 5G at home plans out there even if you can’t lock in the lowest price. 5G Home Minternet (yes, that is what they’re calling it) delivers the same speeds — typically between 133-415 Mbps down — and unlimited data as T-Mobile’s 5G home internet, which is unsurprising seeing as how they run on the same network. The difference is that throttling during periods of network congestion kicks in after 1 TB of data on Mint, but after 1.2 TB on T-Mobile. You’ll also miss out on some perks like advanced security features or bundled streaming services that are included in the more expensive T-Mobile plans, but that’s about it. Unfortunately the pricing structure is a bit of a mess. If you have a Mint phone plan and pay for three months of service, it will cost you $30 a month. But that price is only for new customers, and renewing for three more will cost you $40 a month. If you opt for a six month plan, it will set you back $35 a month. You’ll have to pay for 12 months up front to maintain the $30 per month pricing. The service costs $10 more per month if you’re skipping a phone plan and only getting home internet. Which means this supposedly $30 a month 5G home internet could actually end up costing you $50 per month depending on how you sign up. Still, with no contracts and no need to have a technician come and drill holes in your walls, it might be a decent option depending on where you live.

articles.title: Meta sued over AI smart glasses' privacy concerns, after workers reviewed nudity, sex, and other footage | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Lawyers say Meta's marketing materials promised privacy and user control over sharing footage. But an investigation found that subcontractors are reviewing footage from customers' glasses.
articles.body:
Meta is facing a new class action lawsuit over its AI smart glasses and their lack of privacy, after an investigation by Swedish newspapers found that workers at a Kenya-based subcontractor are reviewing footage from customers’ glasses, which included sensitive content, like nudity, people having sex, and using the toilet.

Meta claimed it was blurring faces in images, but sources disputed that this blurring consistently worked, reports noted . The news prompted the U.K. regulator, the Information Commissioner’s Office, to investigate the matter.

Now, the tech giant is facing a lawsuit in the United States, as well. In the newly filed complaint , plaintiffs Gina Bartone of New Jersey and Mateo Canu of California, represented by the public interest-focused Clarkson Law Firm, allege that Meta violated privacy laws and engaged in false advertising.

The complaint alleges that the Meta AI smart glasses are advertised using promises like “designed for privacy, controlled by you,” and “built for your privacy,” which might not lead customers to assume their glasses’ footage, including intimate moments, was being watched by overseas workers. The plaintiffs believed Meta’s marketing and said they saw no disclaimer or information that contradicted the advertised privacy protections.

The suit charges Meta and its glasses manufacturing partner Luxottica of America with conduct that violates consumer protection laws.

Clarkson Law Firm, which over the years has filed other major lawsuits against tech giants, including Apple , Google , and OpenAI , points to the scale of the issues at hand. In 2025, over seven million people bought Meta’s smart glasses. The footage from those glasses is fed into a data pipeline for review, and users can’t opt out.

Meta told the BBC that when people share content with Meta AI, it uses contractors to review the information to improve people’s experience with the glasses, which is explained in its privacy policy, and it pointed to its Supplemental Meta Platforms Terms of Service , without specifying where this was noted. The news outlet, however, found that a mention of human review could be found in Meta’s U.K. AI terms of service .

A version of that policy that applies to the U.S. states: “In some cases, Meta will review your interactions with AIs, including the content of your conversations with or messages to AIs, and this review may be automated or manual (human).”

The complaint mainly points to how the glasses were marketed, showing examples of ads that touted the privacy benefits, describing their privacy settings, and “added layer of security.”

“You’re in control of your data and content,” one ad read, explaining that the smart glasses owners got to choose which content was shared with others.

The rise of smart glasses and other “luxury surveillance” tech, like always-listening AI pendants, has prompted a broad backlash. One developer published an app capable of detecting when smart glasses are nearby .

Meta did not have a comment on the litigation itself on Thursday morning. However, spokesperson Christopher Sgro offered the following statement about the overall issue, saying, “Ray-Ban Meta glasses help you use AI, hands-free, to answer questions about the world around you. Unless users choose to share media they’ve captured with Meta or others, that media stays on the user’s device. When people share content with Meta AI, we sometimes use contractors to review this data for the purpose of improving people’s experience, as many other companies do. We take steps to filter this data to protect people’s privacy and to help prevent identifying information from being reviewed.”

Updated after publication with Meta’s statement.

articles.title: Snap is finally about to ship AR glasses — and they cost a fortune
articles.summary: Specs, Snap’s first consumer augmented reality glasses, will cost $2,195 and are set to launch this fall. They are available for preorder now.
articles.body: Snap is finally launching augmented glasses for the public. Specs, which Snap describes as “a wearable computer built into see-through augmented reality glasses,” will cost $2,195. You can preorder a pair of Specs now at specs.com with a $200 refundable deposit, and Snap says they’re expected to ship “this fall” in the US, UK, and France. This is a big moment for Snap: The company made a big entry into smart glasses with its original Spectacles in 2016, and the company has been toiling away on nonpublic AR versions of Spectacles over the past few years. CEO Evan Spiegel promised the company would launch consumer AR glasses in 2026 and even turned its smart glasses team into a separate business. The company says that Specs are “fully standalone, with no puck and no tether.” (Which is perhaps a jab at Apple’s Vision Pro, which is tethered to a separate battery pack.) They’ll be offered in two sizes, a 47mm model weighing 132g and a 52mm model weighing 136g, and will have removable inserts that Snap says will support “a wide range of prescriptions.” [Image: You probably won’t mistake Specs, with their wide, bold frames, for any of Meta’s smart glasses — Snap clearly picked a design that it wants to stand out. (They’re not my style — I don’t think I can pull off the “snow goggles, but fashionable” look — though maybe Jony Ive might like them.) They have visible light and infrared cameras, and while the Specs are recording, a little LED bar will glow in the middle of the glasses. Both of the lenses will be able to show you content, and Snap says that its display system is powered by a “proprietary liquid crystal on silicon technology” that offers a 51-degree field of view and can show 16 million colors. The lenses can also go from clear to tinted in 10 seconds, Snap says. The Specs have two Snapdragon processors onboard, and while Snap isn’t specifying exactly which ones they are, the company says that one is focused on “computer vision” while the other is focused on running AR Lenses. “Together, they enable fast hand tracking, low latency, and responsive interactions that help digital content feel anchored in the real world,” Snap says. You can also expect up to four hours of battery life on a charge, which Snap says accounts for things like “audio and video playback, AI assistance, Bluetooth notifications, and more.” The Specs come with a charging case that Snap says will offer four more charges for a total of 20 hours of battery. During his keynote at the AWE 2026 conference, CEO Evan Spiegel noted that you can charge the Specs with a cable that snaps magnetically to the side of the glasses — and if you plug in the other side of that cable to something like a phone, computer, or a gaming device, you can stream content from those devices and display it on your Specs. Specs could be interesting, but we haven’t tried them ourselves yet, so we can’t vouch for what it’s like to actually use them day to day. And we don’t know how Specs actually hold up as a product that sits in between something like Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses, which have been a hit, and the Vision Pro, which has not. Nowadays, there are a lot more smart glasses than when Snap first launched Spectacles. The new Specs are launching a year after Meta’s smart glasses with a single display, though Meta hasn’t publicly launched AR glasses yet despite showing off a model it didn’t sell in 2024. And as my colleague Victoria Song recently wrote, most smart glasses still don’t make sense, not to mention the problem that there are growing privacy concerns about smart glasses. Despite all that, Snap is pushing forward with its Specs launch, so we’ll see how they fare when they’re finally available. Update, June 16th: Added details about the charging cable. Correction, June 16th: Meta has not yet publicly launched AR glasses.

articles.title: Netflix Turns Infamous Stanford Prison Experiment into Reality Show with ‘30 Willing Participants’
articles.summary: The unscripted series, inspired by the controversial 1971 experiment, premieres Oct. 21
articles.body:
Netflix's new unscripted series will put 30 participants in a real prison as guards and prisoners

The New Stanford Prison Experiment premieres Oct. 21 and will span six episodes

The series is inspired by the controversial 1971 Stanford Prison Experiment

Netflix is putting a reality-TV spin on one of psychology's most infamous experiments.

The streamer is set to debut The New Stanford Prison Experiment , an unscripted series that will place 30 participants inside a real prison and randomly assign them to play either guards or prisoners, per a release shared with PEOPLE.

The six-episode debut season is scheduled to premiere Oct. 21. Alfred Street Industries is producing the series, with Jane Lipsitz, Dan Cutforth, Nan Strait, Dan Volpe, Jeff Grogan and Mike Odair serving as executive producers.

The series will examine what happens when ordinary people are placed within a structured system of power and assigned opposing roles.

"Thirty willing participants enter a real prison and are randomly assigned as guards or prisoners. Thrust into a system of power, hierarchy, and control, they'll discover whether ordinary people inevitably conform to the roles they're given—or whether empathy, morality, and individuality can withstand the forces pushing them in the opposite direction," the synopsis reads, per the release.

"As the pressure builds and the balance of power begins to shift, the central question feels more urgent than ever: Does power corrupt?" the synopsis continues.

For Lipsitz, the project offered an opportunity to revisit a study she had long found compelling.

"The Stanford Prison Experiment has always fascinated me," Lipsitz said. "Despite its serious ethical flaws, it asked a fundamental question that feels even more relevant today: how does power affect ethical choices?"

She described making the series as an intense experience.

"Getting the opportunity to reimagine this social experiment was one of the most intense, exhilarating — and definitely nail-biting — experiences we've ever had," she said.

"Netflix has always been an incredible supporter of ambitious projects that take risks, push boundaries and tell challenging stories, so we were incredibly grateful to have them as our partners on this one," Lipsitz added in the release.

The new series takes its name and central premise from the Stanford Prison Experiment, which was conducted at Stanford University in August 1971. Led by psychology professor Philip G. Zimbardo, the study was designed to examine the psychological effects of authority and powerlessness in a prison setting, according to Stanford University .

Researchers recruited Stanford students through a local newspaper advertisement, ultimately selecting 24 students who were screened and randomly assigned to groups of prisoners and guards, according to the university.

Never miss a story — sign up for PEOPLE's free daily newsletter to stay up-to-date on the best of what PEOPLE has to offer, from celebrity news to compelling human interest stories.

The experiment was initially expected to last one to two weeks but was terminated after just six days as the situation escalated. Prisoners were subjected to cruel and dehumanizing treatment by their fellow students, according to Stanford University.

The experiment became widely known for its findings about the influence of social roles and environments on behavior. Zimbardo described the study as showing how "ordinary college students could do terrible things," according to Stanford University.

A dramatized movie titled The Stanford Prison Experiment was released in 2015, starring Billy Crudup, Michael Angarano and Ezra Miller. The movie was made with Zimbardo's active participation and more closely followed the events of the original study, according to Britannica .

articles.title: Who left 'Dancing With the Stars' last night? 1st celebrity sent home after voting glitch.
articles.summary: Online voting crashed during the Season 35 premiere, forcing the show to count only votes submitted by text.
articles.body:
Dancing With the Stars is back for Season 35 — but one celebrity's bid for the mirror ball trophy has already come to an end.

The ABC show kicked off Tuesday night with a new group of celebrities hoping to follow in the footsteps of Season 34 champion Robert Irwin.

This year's cast includes reality TV stars, actors, athletes, musicians and familiar faces from across the entertainment industry, including Summer House star Ciara Miller, 10 Things I Hate About You actor Julia Stiles, The Traitors ' Maura Higgins and singer Taylor Hanson.

Carrie Ann Inaba, Derek Hough and Bruno Tonioli are back at the judges' table, with Alfonso Ribeiro and Julianne Hough returning as hosts for their fourth consecutive season.

But after the first round of performances — and the season's first elimination — the competition has already narrowed. So, who was the first celebrity sent home? Here's what happened.

Who was eliminated from 'Dancing With the Stars' last night?

Secret Lives of Mormon Wives star Conner Leavitt and professional dance partner Adele Zaikman were the first pair eliminated from Season 35.

Leavitt and Zaikman performed a salsa to Tag Team's "Whoomp! (There It Is)," receiving 4s from all three judges for a total score of 12 out of 30.

"This has been the most fun," Leavitt said after being voted off. "I have the greatest dance partner in the world in Adele. I can't wait for the world to get to see her talent."

Zaikman added, "It's a dream come true no matter what, and I'm so lucky that I had Conner. I had so much fun, and thank you so much for everything."

Leavitt's wife, Whitney, reached the semifinals on DWTS last year. Zaikman joined the lineup after winning the inaugural season of spinoff show Dancing With the Stars: The Next Pro .

What happened with 'Dancing With the Stars' voting?

Tuesday night's premiere was hit by technical problems when the show's online voting system crashed during the live broadcast.

Hough initially told viewers that online voting was temporarily unavailable and encouraged them to vote by text. Ribeiro later announced that online votes would be thrown out for the night, meaning only votes submitted by text would count.

Who topped the 'Dancing With the Stars' leaderboard?

Glee star Harry Shum Jr. and professional partner Jenna Johnson finished at the top of the leaderboard Tuesday night, earning 21 out of 30 for their cha cha to Earth, Wind & Fire's "Let's Groove."

Paralympic gold medalist Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach were close behind with 20 points for their tango to Kelly Clarkson's "Since U Been Gone."

The Bachelorette 's Tyler Cameron and Sharna Burgess scored 17 for their tango to Lenny Kravitz's "Are You Gonna Go My Way," while Taylor Hanson and Britt Stewart and Connor Wood and Rylee Arnold each earned 16.

Jackson Olson and Emma Slater scored 15, followed by Leavitt and Zaikman's 12.

Guillermo Rodriguez and Witney Carson finished at the bottom of the judges' leaderboard with 10 points for their cha cha to Jean Knight's "Mr. Big Stuff," but advanced to the next round.

When is 'Dancing With the Stars' on again?

The Season 35 premiere continues Wednesday, Sept. 16, at 8 p.m. ET on ABC and Disney+, when the female celebrities make their competition debuts.

Following the two-night premiere, Dancing With the Stars will air Tuesdays at 8 p.m. ET on ABC and Disney+. Episodes are available to stream the following day on Hulu.

images.caption: Dancing With the Stars is back on ABC for Season 35. (Eric McCandless via Getty Images)
Conner Leavitt and his pro partner, Adele Zaikman, were sent home from DWTS . (Eric McCandless via Getty Images)

articles.title: iOS 27 is here: 10 iPhone features you’ll want to try now
articles.summary: Safari's Notify Me can monitor websites for price changes and restocks, while new AI photo tools let you reframe and extend shots in iOS 27.
articles.body: Your iPhone is getting a major update. Apple released iOS 27 to the public on Monday, Sept. 14, bringing a wave of new features along with the long-awaited Siri AI beta. However, there is much more happening under the hood. Safari can now watch websites for changes. The Photos app gets powerful new editing tools. Apple also says it has made iOS faster across compatible iPhones. Some of these changes could save you from digging through apps or hunting for information yourself. Others give you more control over how your iPhone looks and works. Here are the iOS 27 features I think are worth trying first, along with how to find them. NEW! Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better healthcare With AI In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you take a more active role in your healthcare. You’ll learn how to organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare questions for your next doctor’s visit. No technical experience is needed. Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com 8 BIGGEST THINGS WE LEARNED FROM APPLE'S 2026 EVENT Will your iPhone get iOS 27? The good news is that Apple kept support fairly broad. iOS 27 works with the iPhone 11 family and newer models. It also supports the second-generation iPhone SE and later. That means plenty of people can upgrade without buying a new phone. However, the biggest AI features have tougher hardware requirements. Apple Intelligence and Siri AI require an iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 15 Pro Max, or an iPhone 16 model or later. So, an iPhone 11 can run iOS 27, but it will miss Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features. Keep in mind that many of the features below, including the new AI photo tools, Safari Notify Me and Call Context, also require an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPhone. Siri AI is rolling out in beta in English on supported devices. Apple says support for additional languages will follow later. Availability can also vary by region. iOS 27 should also feel faster Apple says iOS 27 brings performance improvements across the system. In Apple's testing, apps can launch up to 30% faster, new photos can load in the Photos app up to 70% faster and AirDrop transfers can be up to 80% faster. Apple also says iOS 27 improves transitions between Wi-Fi and cellular connections and makes Mail search more relevant. Those are Apple's own figures, so your results will vary depending on your iPhone and how you use it. How to install iOS 27 on your iPhone Before installing a major update, I recommend backing up your iPhone. Also, connect to Wi-Fi and make sure you have enough battery life or plug your phone into power. Then follow these steps: If iOS 27 does not appear immediately, check again later. Apple software releases can take some time to appear on every compatible iPhone. 1) Reframe a photo after you take it Apple Intelligence moves deeper into the Photos app with Spatial Reframing. It lets you change the composition and perspective of a photo after you took it. Apple Intelligence can generate additional parts of the scene when your new framing exposes areas that were outside the original shot. How to use Spatial Reframing Because AI may create new portions of the scene, I would zoom in and inspect the result before sharing an edited photo. Generative tools can still produce odd details. 2) Extend a photo beyond its original edges Maybe you took a photo too close to your subject. The new Extend tool lets you expand beyond the original edges while Apple Intelligence generates the missing surroundings. How to use Extend in Photos The feature will not work with every photo. Apple also says its intelligent photo-editing tools can be subject to daily usage limits. 3) Clean Up can remove bigger distractions Apple has also upgraded Clean Up in Photos. The tool can now tackle larger unwanted objects and distractions while using AI to fill in the space left behind. How to use Clean Up This could be especially handy for removing a person in the background or another distraction that pulls attention away from the subject. Image Playground gets much more realistic Apple is also giving Image Playground a major upgrade in iOS 27. You can now generate images in many more styles, including photorealistic ones. You can also start with an existing image and describe how you want Apple Intelligence to change it. For example, you could ask it to change the setting or adjust the overall look without starting from scratch. As with Apple’s other generative image tools, usage limits may apply. I would also look closely at the results before sharing them, especially when people or detailed objects appear in the scene. 4) Safari can watch a website for you This may end up being one of my favorite iOS 27 features because it solves a very common frustration. Safari’s new Notify Me feature can monitor a webpage for a change you care about. For example, you could ask Safari to watch for a product coming back in stock. It can also monitor a page for a price change. Instead of reopening the same page over and over, Safari can alert you when something changes. How to use Safari Notify Me You can choose hourly, daily, weekly or monthly checks. However, Notify Me does not yet work on every website. Safari can also automatically organize open tabs by topic, which could help anyone whose browser looks like a digital junk drawer by the end of the week. APPLE AI SECURITY UPDATE PROVES HACKERS MOVE FAST 5) Your iPhone can surface information while you are on a call Apple Intelligence is also getting involved when you call businesses. A new feature called Call Context can surface useful information from other apps while you are on a call. Say you call an airline about a reservation. Call Context can pull up a confirmation code from Mail rather than forcing you to leave the Phone app and search for it while someone waits on the other end. There is no complicated workflow to learn. When you place a supported business call and Apple Intelligence identifies relevant information, it can surface that information during the call. Apple says its system determines what could be useful based on who you are calling. It can do that without analyzing the audio from your call. That is the kind of AI feature I want to see more of because you do not have to change your behavior to benefit from it. 6) Liquid Glass gets a much-needed adjustment Last year, Apple introduced the transparent Liquid Glass design across iOS. Some people liked the new look. Others found certain screens harder to read. With iOS 27, Apple says it has improved contrast and readability. More importantly, you now have greater control over how transparent the interface appears. Apple added a slider that lets you move the look from ultraclear toward fully tinted. How to adjust Liquid Glass The changes appear in real time as you move the slider. The setting applies across iOS, including places such as Control Center, notifications and app overlays. This is a small change, but I like that Apple is giving people a choice rather than assuming one visual treatment works for everyone. 7) Put your favorite Camera controls within easy reach If you are always digging around for the timer, exposure or another Camera setting, iOS 27 lets you keep the controls you use most right above the camera frame. Apple starts you with Flash and Live Photo there, but you can customize the row with other tools you use regularly. How to customize your Camera controls Depending on your iPhone and camera mode, available controls can include Flash, Live Photo, Timer, Exposure, Styles and Aspect. Apple also gives you a Reset to Essentials option if you want to return to the default setup. 8) Parents get more control over what kids can open Apple has put a lot of work into parental controls in iOS 27. The new Ask to Browse feature lets a child request access to a website that has been restricted. The parent receives that request through Messages and can approve or decline it. How to set up Ask to Browse You first need Family Sharing set up with your child in the family group. When your child tries to visit restricted web content, they can send an Ask to Browse request for your approval. Apple has also expanded Communication Safety. It already helps protect children from nudity in supported Apple services. With iOS 27, Apple says the system can intervene when it detects gore or violent content in shared photos and videos. 9) Find My gives you more control over location sharing Find My gets a useful privacy upgrade in iOS 27, especially if you only want someone to see your location for a limited amount of time. You can now choose a custom duration for location sharing or set an exact date and time for it to stop. That could come in handy on a trip, during an event or anytime you want temporary location sharing without having to remember to turn it off later. You can also pause location sharing until the end of the day for specific people. Apple says this can be useful when you want to keep something like a surprise party or gift-shopping trip private. How to use the new Find My location options If you already share your location with someone, you can also pause sharing with that person until the end of the day from their location-sharing options. I like having more control here because location sharing often makes sense for a specific situation. You may want someone to know where you are during a weekend trip without giving them indefinite access afterward. 10) You can describe a Shortcut and let AI build it Shortcuts can be incredibly powerful, but building one manually can get complicated fast. iOS 27 makes the process much easier with Describe a Shortcut. You can tell Apple Intelligence what you want your iPhone to automate in plain English. Shortcuts then connects the actions needed to build it. For example, Apple says you could ask your iPhone to message someone with your ETA when you leave work. You could also build automations that work across supported apps. How to create a Shortcut with a description This could make Shortcuts much more approachable for people who have always liked the idea of automating their iPhone but never wanted to figure out how all the individual actions fit together. Some Shortcuts that rely on Apple’s cloud-based AI models may be subject to daily usage limits. ASKED SIRI TO CALL YOUR BANK? A SCAM COULD COST THOUSANDS Bonus: Siri AI is here, but it is still in beta This is the feature many iPhone owners have been waiting for, but I would treat it differently from the 10 features above. Siri AI is rolling out as a beta in English on supported devices, so expect some rough edges while Apple continues to improve it. Siri AI can hold more natural conversations and handle follow-up questions. It can also use personal context from information on your device. For example, you could ask Siri to find an old photo without remembering when you took it. You can also ask it to locate something buried in an email or note. Siri can take more actions inside apps, too. Apple says it can work across messages, emails, photos and other supported apps. Siri can also pull information from the web when you ask broader questions. Why you should care The real test will be whether Siri can save you from bouncing between apps. I have always found voice assistants most useful when they remove a few steps from something I already wanted to do. If Siri AI can reliably find a buried email or pull up a photo from years ago based on a vague description, that could change how often people use it. Because this is still a beta, I would double-check important answers or actions before relying on them. How to try the new Siri AI app Apple has also given Siri its own app, which makes it feel more like the AI assistants people have grown used to using. You can also pin conversations you want to keep handy. Apple says you can invoke Siri AI by saying "Hey Siri," pressing the side button or swiping down from the Dynamic Island on supported iPhones. Kurt’s key takeaways What I like most about iOS 27 is that some of its best features solve problems you actually run into. Safari can keep an eye on a webpage so you do not have to. The new photo tools could rescue a shot you thought was unusable. Find My also gives you better control over how long someone can see your location. I am especially interested in what Apple Intelligence can do with Shortcuts. Describing an automation instead of building it action by action could finally make Shortcuts approachable for people who have always found it too complicated. Siri AI is still the feature I will be watching most closely. Apple is asking us to trust Siri with more personal context and more complicated requests, so getting the answers right will be critical. The fact that Siri AI launches as a beta tells me we should expect some bumps along the way. What I want from AI on my iPhone is pretty simple. Save me time without making me think about the technology doing the work. If iOS 27 can consistently do that, these features could become the ones you use every day without even thinking about them. What would Siri AI have to prove before you let it handle more of your day? articles.title: Xreal’s well-rounded 1S glasses are back down to their lowest price
articles.summary: Solid video glasses get a decent discount. You can also save on the latest Beats Pill, the Sonos Ace, plus numerous Capcom games on Steam.
articles.body: USB-C-connected video glasses are a lot of fun if you want to see your games, movies (or just your computer screen) on a large, immersive virtual screen. One of the most well-rounded pairs out there, Xreal’s 1S, has returned to their lowest price yet, costing $399 at Amazon and via Xreal itself ($50 off). The small, yet welcome discount brings them a little closer in price to the company’s $299 xbx A01 Plus, which lack a handful of nice-to-have features that make the 1S a better choice for some people. The 1S is among the most affordable pairs of video glasses to have three degrees of freedom, letting you anchor the screen to a spot in your room, as opposed to having the screen jolt around with every little movement of your head. Of note, their 3DoF implementation feels less buggy than competitors. They also have much better sound quality than the A01 Plus and most non-Xreal video glasses, plus electrochromic lenses that have adjustable opacity to let in as much (or as little) light as you wish. [Product: Xreal 1S | Not everyone will have a fantastic out-of-the-box experience with the Xreal 1S’ screen clarity. I’m nearsighted, and I needed prescription lenses in order to see things clearly. This model doesn’t offer hardware-based myopia dials like Viture’s $299 Pro 2 does. The Pro 2’s clarity, for me at least, was incredible without lenses, though that pair lacks most of the premium features of the 1S. A few other great Verge-approved deals * The latest version of the Beats Pill Bluetooth speaker has returned to $99.99 (originally $149.99) in every color at Amazon, Best Buy, and Target. It doesn’t often go below this sale price, though it has on rare occasion. While it shares the iconic design of past iterations, former Verge audio reviewer Chris Welch said in his 2024 review that this edition is “more than just a lazy remaster.” It includes lossless audio support over USB-C, and its features work natively across Android and iOS. It can work as a speakerphone, and it sports an IP67 rating, granting it robust protection against water and dust. What’s more, it looks nicer than most of its competitors. * The Sonos Ace Ultra headphones will launch in just a couple weeks, costing $449. It’s how much you’ll have to pay to get wireless headphones that let you swap audio with almost any other Sonos speaker. If you’re alright with the simpler TV Audio Swap feature, its original Ace headphones might be good enough, and refurbished models are almost $200 less than the Ace Ultra. Sonos is selling refurbished (one-year warranty, and in “good as new” condition) Ace headphones for $279 in white or black. Check out our review to see if these sound like a good fit for you. * Those who have a Steam Deck or a gaming PC and are interesting in some affordable games should check out this Capcom-themed game bundle builder at Fanatical. You can buy any two games in the list for $12.99, or add more to get deeper discounts per game. The assortment includes fantastic titles, like many of the latest Resident Evil games (excluding Requiem or the RE4 remake), multi-game collections from the Ace Attorney, Mega Man, and Devil May Cry series, and more. It’s a good opportunity to get caught up on a bunch of Steam games, or round out your collection with two extras.

articles.title: Meta's potential answer to its smart glasses problem? Getting rid of the camera
articles.summary: Meta may be looking to counter backlash to its smart glasses by releasing a pair without cameras.
articles.body:
Meta currently dominates the budding smart glasses market, but that position has made it a lightning rod for public backlash against what some have dubbed "creep glasses." Now, it looks like the company may respond by launching a pair of glasses without built-in cameras. That's according to a new report from The Information , which claims the new glasses could debut next week at Meta's Connect developer conference, which takes place on September 23 and 24.

According to the report, the new glasses are called Luna, and Meta is aiming to start shipping them as soon as October. Though they'll lack cameras, they'll still have six microphones on board, along with a pair of speakers for the wearer to interact with Meta AI. The Information also reports that Luna will have a slimmer design at the temples, making them stand out less compared to regular glasses.

The backlash to Meta's glasses so far has centered around people using them to record and harass people without their permission. Numerous women have reported being recorded without their knowledge by men wearing the glasses. While Meta's glasses have an LED light that turns on while recording to alert people around the wearer, some users modified them to disable it. Meta has since updated its glasses to disable the recording feature if they are modified in this way. They'll also disable recording if the light is covered or obscured.

The prevalence of smart glasses with built-in cameras has even prompted state and city governments to take action. Both New York and Philadelphia have banned smart glasses in courtrooms. Even pop stars are speaking out on them. In July, Lorde told an audience at the Madrid Mad Cool festival, "Can I just say, for the record, f— the glasses. Don't get the glasses. Not sexy."

If Meta launches a new pair of smart glasses without cameras, it's unclear if they'll temper the backlash. Though removing the cameras takes away the biggest issue people have with them, wearers may still be able to record audio of people around them without their knowledge. People might also not know the difference between glasses with and without cameras, so wearers may still be seen as creeps. However, we'll know more if Meta debuts the Luna frames at its Connect conference next week.

images.caption: The updated Meta smart glasses are seen during the Meta Connect event at the company's headquarters in Menlo Park, California, U.S., September 27, 2023. REUTERS/Carlos Barria (REUTERS / Reuters)

articles.title: Your AI agents can now control your Google Home devices | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Google is launching early access to a new MCP server for Google Home, allowing AI agents like Claude, ChatGPT, and others to control connected devices, review camera summaries, and access smart home activity using natural language.
articles.body:
Smart home owners will soon be able to control their devices connected to Google Home via an AI agent. On Tuesday, Google rolled out early access to its Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for its Google Home ecosystem, which will allow any AI agent that supports MCP — like Claude, Hermes, OpenClaw, ChatGPT, and Google Antigravity — to securely work with their smart home devices and access their event history.

This update will allow people to use natural language instructions to do things like review their camera summaries, monitor smart home activity, control their connected devices, and build their own custom smart home dashboards.

To get the connection set up, users will need to create a Google Cloud project and configure it to use Home MCP. They will then provide the MCP configuration details to their agent of choice and ask it to set it up. The agent will then ask them to sign in and grant permissions. (A setup guide will also be offered in the Google Home Developer Center.)

The system will support any device in the Google Home ecosystem, including Google Nest doorbells and thermostats and “Works with Google Home” (or Matter) devices, like light bulbs.

Google already supports MCP in other areas of its business, including in its Google Cloud and data platforms , developer tools, and Google Workspace , for instance. Support for Google Home is targeted more directly at consumers who are experimenting with AI agents designed to handle everyday tasks.

The company said access to the MCP will roll out starting today and continuing over the coming weeks to subscribers who pay for Google Home Premium Advanced in the U.S. This is the more expensive, $20-per-month subscription tier that provides features like longer event-based video history, descriptive notifications and detailed alerts, tools to search video history, daily summaries, and more.

Google wouldn’t comment on if or when the MCP would roll out more broadly, such as to other subscription tiers or markets.

Google is also soliciting feedback from early adopters during this period by way of its Smart Home for Developers Community , it says.

articles.title: Walmart takes a bite off the cost of Metroid Ravenous physical preorders
articles.summary: Walmart is once again giving gamers a discount when they preorder an upcoming Nintendo game, this time taking $10 off Metroid Ravenous.
articles.body: The Metroid series is going back to its 2D roots again with Metroid Ravenous for the Nintendo Switch 2, the first side-scrolling game in the series since 2021’s Metroid Dread for the Nintendo Switch. If you’re already excited enough to consider preordering, you can save $10 on the physical version of the game when you buy it from Walmart. It’s $59.88 instead of $69.99, about the same as buying it digitally. The game launches on January 28th, 2027, but it’s not clear how long the preorder discount will last. If it’s anything like other Walmart preorders, it may occasionally disappear. [Product: Metroid Ravenous | Nintendo first showed off the side-scrolling adventure game at its September 2026 Direct, with a frantic trailer cutting between cinematic sequences, Samus dashing and rolling across a variety of environments, and engaging a number of enemies and bosses in battle. Samus absorbs some powerful abilities at the conclusion of Dread, and Ravenous seem to be all about plowing through anyone stopping her from escaping the planet. Other details of the story, including unique new mechanics, are being kept under wraps for the time being. If you haven’t played Metroid Dread, I recommend it, especially at its $41.99 discounted price at Amazon. It’s part of Nintendo’s “Customer Appreciation” sale happening through September 26th, and several other games and accessories are cheaper, too.

articles.title: I wore Snap’s $2,200 smart glasses
articles.summary: The Verge tried Snap’s Specs AR glasses at the company’s headquarters, and they’re strange glasses with weird ideas.
articles.body: My favorite part of wearing the Specs, Snap’s new augmented reality glasses, was playing dominoes. Sitting across the table from a Snap employee wearing the same pair of chunky glasses, I could select a virtual domino with a pinch and then move my hand to drop it in place, watching the tile snap down in front of us on a real table. It was unlike anything I’ve tried in other VR headsets or smart glasses — the ability to sit with another person and have a shared digital experience. Snap really believes in AR glasses. The company has spent more than half a decade developing the technology, producing two generations of glasses that only ever shipped to a small number of developers. The company seems to want to untether itself from the limitations of being just one app in a big store and instead pioneer the next great platform. Now, Snap is nearly ready to launch its first pair of AR glasses for consumers, the Specs, sometime this fall. That suggests Snap thinks these meet its vision well enough for regular people to enjoy using the $2,195 glasses. They’re certainly full of big ideas. But after an afternoon of testing at Snap’s offices this week, I’m skeptical of whether they’ll be fully ready for primetime. [Image: The Specs are big, black, bold glasses that come in two lens sizes, 47mm and 52mm. Part of why they’re so bold is almost certainly to make a statement — there’s no mistaking these for a regular pair of glasses, like you might with Meta’s Ray-Bans. (They’re a little too conspicuous for me personally; my glasses style is squarely “Elder Millennial Who Shops At Warby Parker.”) But they’re also so chunky because they house all the hardware necessary to let the Specs function as a standalone computer, meaning they don’t need to be tethered to a phone, compute puck, or external battery. They may be chunky, but the Specs aren’t quite as heavy as they look. They’re heavier than my Warby Parker glasses, of course, which I can comfortably wear for most of the day. But the Specs didn’t drag on my face like a full-on VR headset. The Specs felt sturdy, too: I shook my head around and they didn’t fall off or even really slip. I wouldn’t suggest playing pickup basketball in these, but they’ll stay on your face while walking around. They made my ears sag just a little, though. And I wasn’t able to use the Specs enough to tell you if they’d start to feel uncomfortable over the course of a full four-hour battery cycle. Actually using the Specs is kind of like using a hybrid of smart glasses and a VR headset. In front of your eyes, you can see menus, app windows, and elements of whatever app (“lens”) you’re using, like the digital dominoes. Those elements appear over whatever you’re looking at with your eyes through the lenses of the glasses, which have waveguide displays that can show “16 million colors” and “sharp, high-resolution visuals” (Snap hasn’t specified the exact resolution). [Image: Thanks to hand-tracking tech in the Specs, you can pinch and drag to manipulate parts of the interface, such as resizing a window or moving a domino onto the game board, and Snap says you can even snap your fingers to take a picture in the Specs’ Snapchat app. Clever. You can also have windows follow along as you move your head, in case you want to keep a window in your vision no matter where you’re looking. You can access a home button, a Control Center-like menu, and status information like the time by holding up your palm in a setup that reminds me of the ill-fated Humane Pin. In my limited testing, it was all rather finicky. I often had to pinch a few times or make sure my hand was placed in just the right spot to get something to work the way it should. I never quite nailed the two-part action of flipping my hand up and then using my other hand to press the home button. While standing in the sun, it was much harder to see the augmented reality graphics. Snap has beaten competitors like Meta to shipping a pair of glasses with displays in both lenses, letting it deliver a true AR effect and not just another flat screen. But by putting the AR display dead center in your vision, the Specs’ 51-degree field of view becomes a major limitation. It meant that digital elements kept slipping out of sight during my demos, which ruined the illusion that they were actually in the real world. While watching Lanterns on HBO Max in a browser in a moving car, I had to shrink the window to make it easier to see in front of me. While playing dominoes, I had to keep physically turning my head to see my dominoes and the playing board and back again. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: Because it’s 2026, the Specs also have a dedicated AI chatbot assistant, but in my limited experience it was slow and inconsistent. With a “Hey Specs” command, I asked it to show me funny cat videos on YouTube, as suggested by a Snap rep. I had to ask it twice because it didn’t pick up the command the first time. When the command worked, it then took about 15 seconds for the Specs to pull up a YouTube page with search results for funny cat videos. Watching that video also revealed to me a bizarre social interaction that people will have to come to grips with if AR glasses gain any sort of traction. On that YouTube page, I picked some random cat video collection, and it played in the background while the Snap rep kept talking to me. Even though the Specs were playing audio through the onboard speakers, the Snap rep standing right next to me said they couldn’t hear anything. That made me feel weird — these glasses theoretically let you watch and listen to a private video while staring somebody else straight in the eye. Even when I wasn’t watching the video, I found myself constantly distracted from the in-person conversations I was having during the demo because my eyes were caught up with what they were looking at while my hands were focused on arcane gestures for tasks that only I could see. I didn’t feel very present. Like Meta glasses, which are currently grappling with a “pervert” glasses reputation, the Specs also let you take photos and record video. They too have a privacy indicator light, and it’s arguably more prominent than Meta’s take: Instead of a light that’s off to the side, the Specs’ light is right in the center of the glasses. But I don’t know if, given the growing pushback against Meta’s glasses, a blinking light is enough to deter concerns about potential unwanted recording. [Image: That bar in the middle is the privacy indicator light. In 2024, Snap CEO Evan Spiegel told The Verge that there is an opportunity for computers to evolve to “support the ways that humans have long interacted socially by looking at each other eye to eye with much more natural interaction.” Today, Snap has a simpler message: It says that its vision with Specs is to “make computing more human.” But even in my controlled demos, I found that Specs were actually more computer than other hardware; the glasses are unmissable on my head, and the digital content that only I could see was getting in the way of me interacting with the other people in the room. Still, these headsets are coming. Meta is working on a pair, Google has a new glasses initiative, OpenAI has reportedly considered smart glasses, and Apple is apparently planning to announce Ray-Ban Meta-like smart glasses next year (and it’s worth noting that former Apple CEO Tim Cook has repeatedly praised AR in the past). It’s clear they all see the next frontier as glasses with tech like cameras and screens that sit on your head. Specs will be the first real test of what AR glasses can be. But even after Snap’s years of work, they still might be coming out too soon.

articles.title: Snap tries to make the case again for its $2,200 smart glasses | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Since Specs' debut earlier this year, Snap has clearly been looking for an opportunity to explain why the smart glasses deserve to exist.
articles.body:
When Snap debuted its long-awaited smart glasses, Specs, earlier this year, the reveal was not only underwhelming but also a genuine disaster. The glasses — which cost a whopping $2,200 and are vaguely reminiscent of scuba gear — inspired jeers online and calls for the company’s CEO, Evan Spiegel, to resign. The company’s stock subsequently nosedived .

Since then, Snap has clearly been looking for an opportunity to explain why Specs — a heavy, expensive piece of hardware that most casual consumers will probably be unable to afford — deserves to exist.

This week, the company had its chance to make that argument. At an event in Los Angeles, Spiegel and other Snap executives unveiled a variety of new features and services connected to Specs. The new updates seem clearly designed to help integrate the glasses into a broader array of digital activities and, in doing so, give Specs a clearer sense of purpose.

During Wednesday’s event, Spiegel shared details about a number of the new features. After a trippy promotional video that vaguely brought to mind an ayahuasca hallucination, the CEO took the stage and began a series of live demos.

New entertainment options — Specs can now connect with HBO Max and Spotify — provide a baseline of interactive fun that smart glasses have largely lacked until now.

Yet perhaps the biggest announcement was the launch of Specs Intelligence, which the company calls a new “anticipatory AI” system designed to pair not only with the company’s glasses but also with user devices — including iPhones and Macs. Snap claims that this new system “builds an understanding of your goals, priorities, relationships, and routines from the apps and tools you choose to connect, helping you focus on what matters now while making progress towards your longer-term goals.”

Spiegel called this system an “AI native operating system with intelligence designed around your projects” that helps users “connect the dots across Lenses,” Snap’s term for its AR camera effects, available on both phones and Specs, “so you can get things done while focusing on what matters to you.” In practice, it seems to function more like an AI productivity app that can be used with Snap’s glasses but doesn’t require them.

Snap has also announced a new program called Specs for Enterprise, which allows the device to be integrated into corporate workflows. On Wednesday, the company announced partnerships with a number of different tech companies — including Amazon, Salesforce, Nvidia, and other firms — in an effort to make the device useful to staff at those companies.

What is the real-world utility of this, and who is this service really for? Apparently, the answer is IT technicians. While the actual scenarios in which Specs can be used are a little vague, a demo video played at the event showed an IT technician repairing some hardware with the help of Snap’s new glasses.

“We’re building out mobile device management, security controls, and ways to deploy and manage stacks across teams with the world’s most trusted providers, bringing peace of mind to IT departments,” Spiegel said.

Other announced features were slightly more head-scratching. For instance, one of the new experiences is an app, developed through a partnership with the NBA and WNBA, that allows users to practice basketball and improve their shot via the glasses’ AR capabilities. But, realistically, who is really going to play basketball while wearing heavy goggles on their head?

Also announced Wednesday was a new connectivity package for anyone who wants to use Specs on the go, away from Wi-Fi — like outside the home or office. Sold separately, the package includes a charging case with built-in cellular connectivity. That connectivity, which is being made available via a partnership with Verizon, costs $10 a month for Verizon customers and $20 a month for non-Verizon customers.

Spiegel ultimately framed Specs as a new way to engage with computing in a more human-centric format. “I will say it’s an interesting time to be launching a new computer because things in tech are pretty weird right now,” Spiegel said. “We’re being told that AI will take our jobs, that virtual worlds will replace the real one. Well, no, thank you. We do not accept that future. Making people irrelevant is not progress, and computers should make us more important, not less.”

Snap has repeatedly justified the product’s cringe-inducing cost by characterizing the device as a computer — albeit one you wear on your face. Whether consumers will go for that or not remains to be seen. The company has announced that it is hosting a Specs pop-up in Los Angeles in October before the devices ultimately ship later this fall.

articles.title: Bose’s next open earbuds have more bass, more volume, and more battery life
articles.summary: Bose helped start the clip-on earbud trend, and its second-gen Ultra Open Earbuds deliver improved sound and battery life with a redesigned charging case.
articles.body: Bose announced a new version of its Ultra Open Earbuds that helped kick off the industry trend of clip-on wireless earbuds nearly two-and-a-half years ago. The new Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) feature a subtle redesign with improved performance in both sound quality and battery life. They’re also joined by a new cheaper alternative called the Bose Sport Open Earbuds designed to provide a more secure and stable fit during physical activities. The Bose Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) will be available for preorder on September 19th for $299 with availability starting on October 1st. Color options include black, white smoke, cherry chocolate, olive green, and sky pink. Preorders and availability for the Bose Sport Open Earbuds are the same, but they’re $100 cheaper at $199. Colors include black, white smoke, and eucalyptus green. [Image: The design of the Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) remains mostly the same aside from aesthetic improvements. Like the original version, the new Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) feature a design that clips to your outer ear with a transducer that directs audio into your ear canal with “minimal sound leakage,” Bose claims. There’s still no ANC because these are designed to do the exact opposite and let you hear what’s going on around you while enjoying music or a podcast. In addition to a refreshed design with a new beveled finish on each earbud’s metal cap, the 2nd Gen feature a new driver delivering higher volume with automatic adjustments and deeper bass. A new Cinema Mode simulates a “wider, more immersive soundstage” using Bose’s TrueSpatial technology while keeping dialogue clear and centered. Battery life with the buds alone has been boosted to up to nine hours (from seven hours) with an additional 19.5 hours of playback from the redesigned case that can now stand upright for use on a wireless charger. [Image: An added bumpy texture on the Sport Open Earbuds’ customizable buttons makes them easier to locate by touch. The Bose Sport Open Earbuds take a similar approach with a design that clips to your ear to project sounds inward, but they feature a thinner cuff with a “soft silicone matte finish” providing more grip to keep them in place. Bose says the Sport version will stay secure during head shakes, cartwheels, and running. They also feature automatic volume adjustments that adapt to ambient noise levels to ensure what you’re listening to isn’t drowned out, and the customizable shortcut button on the end of each battery barrel has an added texture, so they’re easier to find while working out. Battery life is rated at up to seven hours of playback plus an additional 22 hours with the wireless charging case.
